bai.moTa: Ripples in curvature travel at the speed of light; LIGO heard them in 2015
bai.yChinh: When two massive bodies orbit each other, spacetime curvature around them changes continually. The disturbance travels outward at the speed of light as a **gravitational wave**. As it passes, it stretches distances in one direction and squeezes them in the perpendicular direction, like a tidal force that reverses direction. The waves carry away energy, so the bodies spiral inward faster and faster until they merge. On 9/14/2015 LIGO measured such a signal for the first time.
bai.giaiThich:
A gravitational wave is a disturbance in curvature traveling at speed $c$. It acts like a **reversing tidal force**: a ring of test particles stretches along one axis and contracts along the other, then reverses. The amplitude is $h = \Delta L/L$; its two polarizations, “+” and “×”, are oriented 45° apart.

The source must have a changing **mass quadrupole**. There is no negative mass, and conservation of momentum rules out dipole radiation. Two orbiting bodies emit waves at **twice their orbital frequency**. As they lose energy and spiral inward, both frequency and amplitude rise, producing a chirp. The mass dependence of the frequency growth rate enters only through the **chirp mass**.

GW150914: 36 + 29 M☉ became 62 M☉, with about 3 M☉c² radiated as waves in about 0.2 seconds. LIGO’s 4 km arms changed by about $4 \times 10^{-18}$ m. GW170817: its waves and gamma rays arrived 1.7 seconds apart after 130 million years of travel. The Hulse–Taylor pulsar had already provided indirect evidence in the 1970s and 1980s.
bai.conSo.1: **10⁻²¹**: the peak amplitude of GW150914 at Earth. LIGO’s 4 km arms changed by about 4 × 10⁻¹⁸ m, about 400 times smaller than a proton’s diameter.
bai.conSo.2: **0.2 seconds**: the GW150914 chirp rose from 35 Hz to 150 Hz in about 8 cycles.
bai.conSo.3: **3 M☉**: the mass converted into wave energy (5.4 × 10⁴⁷ J). The peak power was about 3.6 × 10⁴⁹ W, nearly 200 solar masses’ worth of energy per second.
bai.conSo.4: **200 W**: gravitational-wave power from Earth orbiting the Sun.
bai.conSo.5: **76 microseconds per year**: the amount by which the Hulse–Taylor binary pulsar’s orbital period shortens, as predicted.
bai.conSo.6: **1.7 seconds** after 130 million years of travel: the delay of the gamma rays relative to the gravitational waves from GW170817.
bai.hieuDung: **The grid is a drawing convention.** A gravitational wave does not make space bulge upward. It stretches and contracts distances in directions **perpendicular** to its propagation, as the ring of test particles at the detector shows. The grid height indicates wave strength. The effects on the ring and interferometer are magnified about 10²⁰ times. The two bodies are drawn too large relative to the wavelength, and everything is shown in slow motion.
bai.nguon: GW150914: Abbott et al. (LIGO and Virgo) 2016, Phys. Rev. Lett. 116, 061102 (masses, energy, peak power, distance, amplitude, frequency, and signal delay between detectors). GW170817: LIGO and Virgo 2017 with gamma-ray observatories (masses, distance, 1.7-second delay). Binary pulsar and quadrupole formula: Hartle (2003), ch. 16. Constants: CODATA 2018, IAU 2015. The values are recalculated in kiem-tra/kiem-song-va-gian-no.mjs.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: Explain gravitational waves as reversing tidal forces traveling at the speed of light, and interpret their amplitude $h = \Delta L / L$.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Distinguish “+” and “×” polarizations using a ring of test particles.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Explain why a source needs a changing quadrupole and why the wave frequency is twice the orbital frequency.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Use the frequency growth formula to understand the chirp and the chirp mass.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.5: Describe the key measurements of GW150914, how LIGO works, and the evidence from the binary pulsar and GW170817.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
You are looking at two black holes with 36 and 29 solar masses orbiting each other, based on the actual measurements of GW150914. The grid ripples in spirals of gold and blue that travel outward. These are {{sóng hấp dẫn|gravitational waves}}.

In Lesson 12 we saw spacetime curvature reveal itself through {{lực thủy triều|tidal forces}}. Around a stationary source, curvature stays the same. When two objects orbit each other, the surrounding curvature changes continuously. In relativity that change cannot be communicated instantly. The disturbance spreads outward in successive layers **at exactly the speed of light**, just as an oscillating charge emits electromagnetic waves.

The model calculates this delay. At a distance $r$ from the source, each grid point shows what the source was doing $r/c$ earlier. Distant ripples are therefore an echo of a time when the pair was orbiting more slowly.

> [Lưu ý] The rising and falling grid **represents wave strength**. Space does not bulge in any direction. The two objects are enlarged relative to the wavelength, and everything is shown in **slow motion** (see the factor in the data panel).

> [Thử ngay] [[View from above|tren]] [[View at an angle|nghieng]] [[Replay from the start|lai]]
> Drag the green dot (the detector) around the source, including above the two black holes. The small particle ring at the detector and the signal display above it show how strong the wave is there.

> [Lưu ý] **What you hear** is the detector signal. Pitch matches the wave’s actual frequency and loudness follows amplitude. The visuals are slowed but pitch is preserved; step 5 explains the conversion.

+++ Go deeper: waves as solutions of Einstein’s vacuum equations
Far from the source, spacetime is nearly flat. Write its metric as the flat metric plus a small perturbation: $g = \eta + h$, with $|h| \ll 1$. Substitute into the {{phương trình Einstein|Einstein field equations}} and retain only terms of first order in $h$. In vacuum, with a suitable choice of coordinates, the result is the wave equation

$$ \Big(\frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2} - \nabla^2\Big) h = 0 . $$

Its propagation speed is $c$, with no adjustable parameter. Einstein found this in 1916. In 1918 he obtained the formula for the amount of radiation a source emits (the quadrupole formula in step 4). For decades physicists debated whether the waves really carried energy or were an artifact of the coordinates. Measurements settled the issue: first the binary pulsar (step 8), then LIGO (step 6).
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.de: Drag the detector directly above the black holes, within **10°** of the orbital rotation axis. The wave is strongest there: its “+” amplitude is twice that in the orbital plane. The distorted particle ring rotates and the sound is louder.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.goiY: Drag the green dot upward along the dotted green line. The data panel shows the angle between the detector direction and the rotation axis (purple line).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.ten: A passing wave: tidal forces that reverse
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
The camera has moved to the detector. Above it is a **ring of freely falling test particles** in a plane **perpendicular** to the wave direction (gold arrow). As the wave passes, the ring stretches horizontally and contracts vertically. Half a cycle later the pattern reverses.

This is the picture from Lesson 12, where tides stretched a falling ring of particles around Earth vertically and squeezed it horizontally. The wave’s tidal force **keeps reversing**. The pink arrows show the tidal force on each particle at this instant.

Wave strength is measured by the {{biến dạng h|strain}}. For two particles separated by $L$, the distance changes by an amount of order $\Delta L$, with

$$ h = \frac{\Delta L}{L}. $$

> [Ví dụ] At Earth, the waves from GW150914 had $h \approx 10^{-21}$. Two particles 1 meter apart moved by only $10^{-21}$ m, a million times smaller than an atomic nucleus.

The wave is **transverse**: distances along the direction of propagation do not change.

> [Lưu ý] The ring on screen is distorted by up to 15%, or $h \approx 0{,}3$. This is **magnified by about $10^{20}$ times** relative to the real wave.

> [Thử ngay] [[Slow, steady example|mau]] [[Make the ring follow the actual wave|that]] [[Hide or show tidal forces|tt]]
> Hover over the ring to see how much it stretches in each direction. When the ring follows the actual wave, you hear that signal at its actual frequency. The ring on screen expands and contracts about 73 times more slowly because of the slow-motion display.

+++ Go deeper: particle displacement and the tidal force
Take $x$ as horizontal and $y$ as vertical in the ring plane. The wave travels along $z$. For a “+” polarized wave of amplitude $h_+(t)$, a particle at $(x;\ y)$ is displaced by

$$ \delta x = \tfrac12 h_+ x, \qquad \delta y = -\tfrac12 h_+ y . $$

Differentiate twice with respect to time to obtain the acceleration, or tidal force per unit mass:

$$ a_x = \tfrac12 \ddot h_+ x, \qquad a_y = -\tfrac12 \ddot h_+ y . $$

For a sinusoidal wave, $\ddot h_+ = -\omega^2 h_+$. The force always pulls the particle back toward the circle, like a pendulum. This is why the pink arrows point opposite to the displacement.

There is a direct link to Lesson 12: stretching along $x$ equals squeezing along $y$, so the ring’s area is unchanged to first order. In Lesson 12 the volume of a freely falling ball of particles contracts only through $\rho + 3P/c^2$. In vacuum $\rho = P = 0$, leaving only the curvature that **distorts shape without changing volume**. A gravitational wave is this part of the curvature propagating away from its source.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
The ring can stretch in two independent patterns. The {{phân cực sóng hấp dẫn|“+” polarization}} stretches it horizontally and squeezes it vertically, then reverses. The “×” pattern is identical but rotated **45°**, stretching one diagonal and squeezing the other. Any gravitational wave can be expressed as a sum of these two polarizations.

> [Thử ngay] [[+ polarization|p]] [[× polarization|x]] [[Both, a quarter cycle apart|tron]]
> Drag the yellow dot on the rim to rotate the two detector arms (the perpendicular yellow segments). The difference shown is one arm’s length minus the other’s, precisely what an L-shaped detector measures.

With the third button, the ring becomes a **rotating ellipse**: this is {{phân cực tròn|circular polarization}}. An orbiting pair emits this kind of wave along the rotation axis. In the orbital plane only the “+” polarization remains. The model detector lies in this plane, so it receives only “+”.

Compare light: electromagnetic waves also have two polarizations, but their axes are **90°** apart. Gravitational waves have a 45° separation because the changing quantity is a stretching pattern rather than a vector such as the electric field. Rotate the ring 90° and the “+” pattern changes sign. Rotate 180° and the original pattern returns.

> [Lưu ý] An L-shaped LIGO detector responds most strongly to “+” when its arms align with the stretching and squeezing axes. With the same arm orientation, “×” distorts the diagonals without changing either arm length, so the detector registers nothing. This is why detectors at different orientations are needed.

+++ Go deeper: why the polarizations are 45° apart
In the plane perpendicular to propagation, the wave is represented by a symmetric matrix whose diagonal entries sum to 0:

$$ h = \begin{pmatrix} h_+ & h_\times \\ h_\times & -h_+ \end{pmatrix}. $$

Such a matrix has only two independent numbers: the two polarizations. Rotating the axes through $\theta$ transforms the components as

$$ h_+' = h_+\cos 2\theta + h_\times \sin 2\theta, \qquad h_\times' = -h_+\sin 2\theta + h_\times\cos 2\theta . $$

The angle occurs as $2\theta$. A rotation of $45°$ converts “+” into “×”, $90°$ reverses the sign, and $180°$ restores the pattern. For an electromagnetic wave the electric field is a vector and transforms with $\theta$ instead of $2\theta$, so its polarizations are separated by $90°$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.de: For “×” polarization, horizontal and vertical arms register nothing. Rotate the arms until their length difference is **greatest** (within 4°). What is that angle?
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.goiY: The “×” polarization stretches and squeezes along the ring’s diagonals, marked by faint diagonal lines. Keep “Example: ×” selected in the controls.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.ten: A quadrupole source: two wave cycles per orbit
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
Look down from above. The ripples spiral outward in **two arms**. After the two objects complete half an orbit the pattern looks the same, like a rotating dumbbell. Each orbit therefore produces **two** wave cycles:

$$ f_\text{sóng} = 2 f_\text{quỹ đạo}. $$

The data panel shows this directly: the number of orbits per second is always half the wave frequency.

Why is there no simpler radiation pattern? Electromagnetic waves can come from a {{lưỡng cực|dipole}}, with positive and negative charges oscillating in opposite directions. For gravity:

- The **monopole** is the total mass, including energy. It is conserved and cannot oscillate.
- The mass **dipole** equals the total mass times the center-of-mass position. There is no negative mass to separate the poles. To oscillate, the center of mass would have to accelerate on its own, changing the total momentum. Conservation of momentum forbids that.
- The **quadrupole** describes the *shape* of the mass distribution: how flattened or elongated it is, and in which direction. This is the lowest order that can oscillate. A rotating dumbbell changes its quadrupole continuously.

> [Thử ngay] [[Slow down|cham]] [[Freeze|dung]] [[Normal speed|thuong]] [[View the pair up close|gan]]
> Drag the yellow dot on the ruler to set the separation; the model pauses while you drag. Hover over a black hole to read its speed.

> [Con số] Earth orbiting the Sun emits gravitational waves too: two cycles per year at a power of about **200 W**, comparable to a light bulb. Strong emission requires large masses orbiting very fast and very close together.

+++ Go deeper: the quadrupole formula and why the waves are so weak
Einstein showed in 1918 that at distance $r$ the wave amplitude is proportional to the second time derivative of the mass quadrupole $Q$,

$$ h \sim \frac{2G}{c^4}\,\frac{\ddot Q}{r}. $$

The coefficient $G/c^4 \approx 8 \times 10^{-45}$ in SI units is extremely small: spacetime is very “stiff.” For masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ in a circular orbit at separation $a$, the radiated power is

$$ P = \frac{32}{5}\,\frac{G^4}{c^5}\,\frac{(m_1 m_2)^2 (m_1 + m_2)}{a^5}. $$

Substituting Earth’s mass ($6{,}0 \times 10^{24}$ kg), the Sun’s mass ($2{,}0 \times 10^{30}$ kg), and $a = 1{,}5 \times 10^{11}$ m gives $P \approx 196$ W. Over 4.6 billion years, Earth has lost negligible energy to gravitational waves compared with its orbital energy. But $P$ is proportional to $1/a^5$: two black holes hundreds of kilometers apart can radiate more power by dozens of orders of magnitude.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Drag the ruler until the two black holes complete exactly **25 orbits per second** (within 1 orbit per second), then hold it there. What is the wave frequency in hertz?
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: The data panel shows “wave frequency = 2 × orbits per second.” The target separation is about 700 km. Hold the mouse still for half a second, or release it and click “Freeze”.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.ten: Losing energy and spiraling inward: the chirp
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
The waves carry energy away. As the bodies lose energy they drop to a lower orbit, where they **orbit faster** (Kepler’s law: $\omega^2 = GM/a^3$). Faster orbital motion means stronger radiation and an even faster inward spiral. The process accelerates until the two bodies touch.

The signal rises in **both frequency and amplitude** and sweeps sharply upward at the end. Physicists call it a “chirp,” like a bird call. The graph beneath the controls records that shape. The frequency growth rate is

$$ \frac{\dd f}{\dd t} = \frac{96}{5}\,\pi^{8/3} \left(\frac{G\mathcal{M}}{c^3}\right)^{5/3} f^{11/3}, $$

$$ \mathcal{M} = \frac{(m_1 m_2)^{3/5}}{(m_1+m_2)^{1/5}} . $$

Here $f$ is the wave frequency and $\mathcal{M}$ is the {{khối lượng chirp|chirp mass}}. The two masses enter through this one combination, so **measuring $f$ and $\dd f/\dd t$ determines $\mathcal{M}$**.

> [Ví dụ] At 35 Hz, GW150914 had $\dd f/\dd t \approx 79$ Hz per second, corresponding to $\mathcal{M} \approx 30$ M☉ as measured at the detector. From 35 Hz to merger only about 0.17 seconds remained.

> [Thử ngay] Change the pair and watch and listen to its chirp. Neutron stars are lighter and spiral together much more slowly.
> [[GW150914 (black holes)|ld]] [[GW170817 (neutron stars)|nt]] [[Two black holes, 10 + 10 M☉|muoi]]
> Drag the dots on the two columns to change the individual masses on a logarithmic scale. Each change restarts the model.

> [Lưu ý] **The audio is a conversion of the signal**: gravitational waves are not sound waves traveling through space. At each frame the sound frequency equals the wave frequency $f$ at the corresponding instant, and loudness is proportional to $f^{2/3}$, as is the amplitude $h$. The model plays about 73 times more slowly for GW150914, but **preserves pitch** instead of lowering it by a factor of 73. Dividing 35 Hz by 73 would give an inaudible 0.5 Hz. Only the duration is stretched. “Listen in real time” plays the last 0.2 seconds at the actual pitch and rate. Small computer speakers struggle below 100 Hz; select “Raise by two octaves” to multiply the frequency by 4.

+++ Go deeper: deriving the formula in three lines
The energy of a circular orbit is $E = -\dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{2a}$. Kepler’s law gives $\omega^2 = \dfrac{GM}{a^3}$ with $M = m_1 + m_2$. Eliminate $a$:

$$ E = -\tfrac12 \,\mu\, (GM\omega)^{2/3}, \qquad \mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{M}. $$

Express the quadrupole power from step 4 in terms of $\omega$: $P = \dfrac{32}{5}\dfrac{G}{c^5}\mu^2 a^4 \omega^6$. Noting that $\mu M^{2/3} = \mathcal{M}^{5/3}$ gives

$$ E = -\tfrac12 (G\mathcal{M}\omega)^{2/3}\,\mathcal{M}, \qquad P = \frac{32}{5}\,\frac{(G\mathcal{M}\omega)^{10/3}}{G\,c^5}. $$

Set $\dd E/\dd t = -P$:

$$ \frac{\dd \omega}{\dd t} = \frac{96}{5}\left(\frac{G\mathcal{M}}{c^3}\right)^{5/3} \omega^{11/3}. $$

The wave frequency is $f = 2 \times \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \omega/\pi$. Substituting gives the formula above. Solving this equation, let $\tau$ be the time left before contact; then $f \propto \tau^{-3/8}$. A decrease in the remaining time by a factor of 256 raises the frequency by only a factor of 8. This is why the signal lasts so long at low frequencies and rises so abruptly at the end. The amplitude obeys $h \propto \mathcal{M}^{5/3} f^{2/3}/d$.

The formula applies only while the bodies are still far apart. The last few orbits and the merger require numerical solutions of Einstein’s equations. As an illustration, the model holds frequency constant in the final segment and lets the newly formed black hole ring down.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.de: Change the two black hole masses until the chirp reaches **250 Hz** at merger (within 10 Hz). The data panel and the card in the controls show the merger frequency. What is the total mass?
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.goiY: In this model the merger frequency is inversely proportional to total mass: heavier black holes are larger and touch while orbiting more slowly. GW150914 (65 M☉) merges at about 150 Hz.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
On **9/14/2015**, the two LIGO detectors in Livingston and Hanford in the US, 3,000 km apart, recorded the same chirp. Livingston received it about 7 milliseconds earlier. This is less than the 10 milliseconds light takes to travel between the sites, consistent with a wave traveling at speed $c$.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Initial black holes | 36 and 29 M☉ |
| Final black hole | 62 M☉ |
| Radiated as waves | about 3 M☉, or $5{,}4 \times 10^{47}$ J |
| Frequency | 35 → 150 Hz in about 0.2 s, roughly 8 cycles |
| Peak power | about $3{,}6 \times 10^{49}$ W |
| Distance | about 410 Mpc, roughly 1.3 billion light-years |
| Peak amplitude at Earth | $h \approx 10^{-21}$ |

The peak power corresponds to nearly **200 solar masses’ worth of energy per second**, about $10^{23}$ times the Sun’s power. At a wave frequency of 150 Hz the holes were only about 340 km apart and orbited one another at about half the speed of light. The wavelength then was $c/f \approx 2\,000$ km, five hundred times the length of a LIGO arm.

> [Thử ngay] [[Replay from the start|lai]] [[Go close to merger|cuoi]] [[Slow down further|cham]] [[Listen in real time|that]]
> The last button plays the model in real time. The final 0.2 seconds flash by, and you hear a short sweep from 35 Hz to about 150 Hz. Drag the separation ruler to move forward or backward.

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “3 solar masses disappeared.” They were converted into **wave energy**, $E = mc^2$, which traveled outward through the universe. Total energy was conserved.

> [Lịch sử] The result was announced on 2/11/2016 (Abbott et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 116, 061102). Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish, and Kip Thorne received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics for their decisive contributions to LIGO and the detection of gravitational waves.

+++ Go deeper: how the numbers in the table fit together
- **Chirp mass.** For 36 and 29 M☉, $\mathcal{M} = (36 \cdot 29)^{3/5}/65^{1/5} \approx 28{,}1$ M☉. Cosmic expansion stretched the waves on their way to us ($z \approx 0{,}09$; see Lesson 18). The detector therefore measures a $\mathcal{M}$ about 9% larger, roughly 30 M☉. This is the value used in step 5.
- **Time.** The chirp formula gives 0.16 seconds and about 8.5 wave cycles from 35 Hz to 150 Hz, in agreement with the observed signal.
- **Energy.** $3\ \text{M☉} \times c^2 = 3 \times 1{,}99 \times 10^{30} \times (3 \times 10^8)^2 \approx 5{,}4 \times 10^{47}$ J. Averaging over 0.2 seconds gives $2{,}7 \times 10^{48}$ W. Peak power is about ten times larger because most energy is released during the last few cycles.
- **Amplitude.** The formula $h \propto \mathcal{M}^{5/3} f^{2/3}/d$ gives $h \approx 2{,}4 \times 10^{-21}$ at 150 Hz for a view directly along the orbital axis. The actual system was tilted and the detector was not oriented directly toward it, so the observed peak was smaller: $1{,}0 \times 10^{-21}$.
+++

bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.goiY: The frequency rises very quickly near the end. Drag very slowly once the black holes are close.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.ten: The LIGO interferometer: measuring less than a proton’s diameter
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
At the detector you now see a LIGO-type {{giao thoa kế|interferometer}}. The laser beam (gold) reaches a **beam splitter** and divides in two. The beams travel along perpendicular **arms**, reflect from the **end mirrors**, and meet again. The instrument is adjusted so the beams cancel and the output port is **dark**.

When a “+” wave passes, one arm lengthens and the other shortens. The relative phase of the returning beams changes, so they no longer cancel completely, and **light reaches the photodetector**. Its brightness varies with the wave.

> [Thử ngay] [[Follow the real wave|that]] [[Slow example oscillation|mau]] [[Freeze|dung]]

Each LIGO arm is **4 km** long. For $h = 10^{-21}$, the length difference between the arms is

$$ \Delta L = h L = 10^{-21} \times 4\,000\ \text{m} = 4 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{m}, $$

about **400 times** smaller than a proton’s diameter ($1{,}7 \times 10^{-15}$ m).

Several features make this measurable. Light bounces back and forth hundreds of times within each arm, so the phase shift accumulates. The laser is powerful and stable. Mirrors weighing tens of kilograms hang from vibration isolation systems. Two widely separated instruments provide a check: a signal must appear in both.

> [Lưu ý] Changes in arm length are magnified about $10^{20}$ times in this drawing. The output brightness illustrates a dark port at rest and a brighter one during a wave; it does not reproduce the actual brightness.

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “The wave stretches the light too, so light cannot serve as a ruler.” Light already traveling in an arm is also affected, but the laser continuously supplies new light at a fixed frequency. LIGO compares the light’s **round-trip travel times** in the two arms. Those times really do change.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.ten: Other evidence and new ways to listen
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
**The Hulse–Taylor binary pulsar.** In 1974 Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor discovered a pulsar orbiting another neutron star with an orbital period of **7.75 hours**. A pulsar is an exceptionally regular clock, allowing the orbit to be measured precisely. Over many years the orbital period shortened by about **76 microseconds per year**, in agreement with the quadrupole formula. This was the first indirect evidence that gravitational waves carry energy away (Nobel Prize, 1993).

**GW170817.** On 8/17/2017 two neutron stars merged 130 million light-years away. Their small chirp mass (about 1.19 M☉) produced a chirp lasting **about 100 seconds** in LIGO’s frequency band. Then **1.7 seconds** after merger, satellites detected a gamma-ray burst from the same direction. After 130 million years of travel, the signals arrived only 1.7 seconds apart: the speed of gravitational waves matches $c$ to about $10^{-15}$. Telescopes also saw a kilonova, an explosion that produces heavy elements such as gold and platinum.

> [Thử ngay] [[Select GW170817|nt]] [[Return to GW150914|ld]]
> Listen: with two lighter neutron stars the chirp is much higher, above 800 Hz even at the start of the modeled segment.

| Detector | Frequency range | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| LIGO, Virgo, KAGRA (ground-based) | about 10 Hz to several thousand Hz | black holes and neutron stars of one to several dozen M☉ |
| LISA (three spacecraft 2.5 million km apart; launch planned for the middle of the 2030s) | millihertz | merging supermassive black holes |
| Pulsar timing arrays | nanohertz (periods of years) | supermassive black hole pairs in galactic centers |

In 2023 pulsar timing arrays reported evidence for a **gravitational-wave background** with periods of years. The next lesson moves from mergers to the universe as a whole. The waves from GW150914 were stretched on their way to us because space itself is expanding.

+++ Go deeper: checking two numbers
**Binary pulsar.** For an elliptical orbit, Peters and Mathews extended the quadrupole formula with a factor depending on eccentricity $e$. Using the stellar masses (1.44 and 1.39 M☉), $e = 0{,}617$, and the period of 7.75 hours gives a period decrease of $2{,}40 \times 10^{-12}$ seconds per second, or about 76 microseconds per year.

**GW170817.** 130 million years is $130 \times 10^6 \times 3{,}16 \times 10^{7} \approx 4{,}1 \times 10^{15}$ seconds. If the full 1.7 seconds arose because gravitational waves traveled faster or slower than light, the speed difference would be only $1{,}7 / 4{,}1 \times 10^{15} \approx 4 \times 10^{-16}$. In reality the gamma rays may have been emitted a little after the merger, so scientists quote a more conservative bound of order $10^{-15}$.
+++

bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.ten: Wave frequency is twice orbital frequency
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: After half an orbit the two-body system looks as it did before.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.ten: Quadrupole power from two bodies in circular orbit
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: Earth orbiting the Sun: about 200 W. Power is proportional to $1/a^5$, so it is appreciable only for compact objects very close together.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.5.y: Measuring $f$ and $\dd f/\dd t$ determines the chirp mass.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: A “+” polarized gravitational wave travels along $z$ through a ring of particles in the $xy$ plane. When the ring is longest along $x$, how long is it along $y$?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: The “+” polarization stretches along one direction and simultaneously squeezes along the perpendicular direction, preserving the ring’s area. Nothing changes along $z$, the propagation direction: gravitational waves are transverse.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: Two neutron stars orbit each other 100 times per second. What is the frequency of their gravitational waves?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: The system looks the same after half a turn, so each orbit produces two wave cycles: $f_\text{sóng} = 2 \times 100 = 200$ Hz.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: Why is there no gravitational dipole radiation like the electromagnetic waves from an antenna?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.2: The mass dipole depends only on the center-of-mass position, and conservation of momentum prevents the center of mass from accelerating on its own
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.3: Gravitational waves travel more slowly than light
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: There is no negative mass, so the mass dipole is simply total mass times center-of-mass position. Its second derivative is the rate of change of total momentum, always 0. A small $G$ makes the waves weak, but does not forbid dipole radiation.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: A wave with $h = 10^{-21}$ passes through a 4 km arm. Roughly how much does its length change?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: $\Delta L = hL = 10^{-21} \times 4 \times 10^{3}$ m $= 4 \times 10^{-18}$ m. A common error is forgetting to convert 4 km to 4,000 m.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: Suppose a merger identical to GW150914 took place twice as far away. How would the amplitude $h$ reaching Earth change?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.2: It would fall to one quarter
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.4: It would fall to one eighth
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: Amplitude falls as $1/d$; energy, proportional to $h^2$, falls as $1/d^2$. A detector twice as sensitive can hear twice as far and survey eight times the volume.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: Explain why the signal from two inspiraling black holes gets higher and louder near the end instead of staying steady.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: Waves carry energy away, so the black holes drop to a smaller orbit. A smaller orbit means faster orbital motion (Kepler), raising the wave frequency, which is twice the orbital frequency. Closer, faster bodies radiate much more strongly (power is proportional to $1/a^5$), and so lose energy even faster. Both frequency and amplitude rise steeply until the holes touch.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapter 16: gravitational waves, the quadrupole formula, the binary pulsar, and interferometers.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: B. Schutz, *A First Course in General Relativity* (2nd edition, 2009): the chapter on gravitational radiation includes interferometric measurement.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: K. S. Thorne, *Black Holes and Time Warps* (1994): the history of gravitational waves and the early days of LIGO, told by one of its founders.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: Abbott et al. (LIGO) 2016, Phys. Rev. Lett. 116, 061102: the paper announcing GW150914.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: Gravitational-wave strength: the ratio $\Delta L / L$ of a change in distance to the distance itself. Waves reaching Earth have $h$ of order $10^{-21}$.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: Two independent deformation patterns: “+” stretches horizontally and squeezes vertically, while “×” does the same after a 45° rotation.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: A superposition of two equal-amplitude polarizations separated in phase by a quarter cycle. The particle ring deforms into a rotating ellipse. An orbiting pair emits this polarization along its rotation axis.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: A distribution with two poles of opposite sign, such as positive and negative charges. Oscillating dipoles are a major source of electromagnetic radiation, but do not produce gravitational dipole radiation.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.5.nghia: Waves produced when the shape of a mass distribution (its quadrupole) varies with time. This is the lowest allowed order of gravitational radiation.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.6.nghia: The mass combination $(m_1 m_2)^{3/5}/(m_1+m_2)^{1/5}$ that sets how fast the frequency rises as two objects spiral together. It can be measured directly from the signal.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.7.nghia: An instrument that splits a light beam in two, sends the beams along different paths, and recombines them. A tiny path difference changes the output brightness.
